ety.text: From Middle English elbowe (“elbow”), from Old English elboga, elnboga (“elbow”), from Proto-Germanic *alinabugô (“elbow”), equivalent to ell + bow. Cognate with Scots elbuck (“elbow”), Saterland Frisian Älbooge (“elbow”), Dutch elleboog (“elbow”), Low German Ellebage (“elbow”), German Ellbogen, Ellenbogen (“elbow”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål albue (“elbow”), Norwegian Nynorsk olboge (“elbow”), Faroese albogi, Icelandic olbogi, olnbogi (“elbow”), Swedish armbåge (“elbow”).

senses.d: The joint between the upper arm and the forearm.
ex: Up to the elbowes naked were there Armes.

senses.d: Any turn or bend like that of the elbow, in a wall, building, coastline, etc.; an angular or jointed part of any structure, such as the raised arm of a chair or sofa, or a short pipe fitting, turning at an angle or bent.
ex: the sides of windows, where the jamb makes an elbow with the window back

senses.d: Part of a basketball court located at the intersection of the free-throw line and the free-throw lane.
A hit, strike, or blow with the elbow.
Two nearby crossings of a rope.
To push with the elbow or elbows; to forge ahead using the elbows to assist.
ex: He elbowed his way through the crowd.
Trumper elbowed me in the ribs and made a sign with his head. He seemed irritated now by our delay.

senses.d: To force (someone) to quit or lose their job so that someone else can be hired.
ex: The president was elbowed out of power by members of her own party.

grp.label: joint between upper arm and forearm

ety.text: Inherited from Old French code, cote, coute, cute, inherited from Latin cubitum, cubitus. Doublet of cubitus.
From earlier gombito, inherited from Latin cubitum, noun use of the neuter of cubitus, the passive perfect participle of cubō (“to lie down, recline”). Doublet of the borrowing cubito.

chain.g: reclined, lying down, having been reclined.

ety.text: Latin cubitusnom. Latin cubitum Old Spanish cobdo Spanish codo Inherited from Old Spanish cobdo, from Latin cubitum (“elbow, cubit”), substantivized from the perfect passive participle of cubō (“to lie down”). Doublet of cúbito (“ulna”), a later borrowed form.

Ultimately from Latin cubitum (“elbow”) through Old Galician-Portuguese *covetelo, either from Latin cubitālis (via Mozarabic qubtal) or alternatively from Latin cubitellum. Cognate with Galician cotobelo. Cf. also the related coto and côvado.
Latin cubitusnom. Latin cubitum Old Spanish cobdo Spanish codo Spanish -azo Spanish codazo From codo + -azo.
